paras: The False River ball shooting was an exchange of gunfire at a Black ball on False River, Pointe Coupee Parish, Louisiana, near midnight on August 13, 1881, in which a white man, L. T. Chenvert, was killed, a white youth, Joseph Garon, was wounded, and several Black men were wounded by shotgun fire. Sixteen Black men were jailed, and two, Val Dorval and Leopold Polite, were held for murder. Every account traces to the local Pointe Coupee Banner or to brief wire dispatches, which blamed the Black men under headlines such as "Murderous Negroes."

On the evening of August 13 young white men and women gathered at the residence of Mrs. J. B. Garon on False River for a "night gumbo." Black residents of upper False River held a ball the same night in a former "negro school-house" about one hundred feet away, on premises occupied by David Johnson, a white man who, the Banner said, had allowed it on condition of good order.

Between eleven and twelve o'clock the Banner reported a "fuss and loud cursing" at the ball, and Johnson, Chenvert and two or three other white men walked over; Johnson told the ball-goers that if they could not behave they would have to quit the premises. In the Banner's telling, after a moment of quiet a Black man fired a pistol into the air, a voice called "come quick boys let's crowd them and give them hell," and the crowd opened fire on the white men across the road.

The Banner said Johnson was the only armed white man; Chenvert took his pistol, fired once and fell dead. While Johnson ran to his house for his shotgun, Garon, about 18, ran from his mother's house with a pistol and was shot through the thigh and again under the shoulder blade. Johnson then fired both barrels of No. 7 shot into the crowd, which scattered. Several Black men were "slightly wounded by bird shot" and one was hit by a ball in the abdomen; the wire said none were killed.

On Sunday a large crowd gathered at New Road, and squads set out in every direction; sixteen Black men were brought to jail, some found hiding in woods and field ditches, while four or five remained at large. The Banner reported stores closed and a white determination that "the guilty shall not escape full measure of punishment." At a preliminary examination the following Friday, Judge Yoist discharged all but Val Dorval and Leopold Polite, who were ordered to answer a charge of murder. No report of an inquest, indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

The Louisiana Capitolian of Baton Rouge reprinted the Banner's August 20 account as "Riot in Pointe Coupee" on August 25 and 27, and the St. Landry Democrat reprinted it on September 3. The Lake Charles Echo condensed it as "Negro Riot and Bloodshed in Pointe Coupee Parish," and the Donaldsonville Chief's editorial "Atrocious Crimes" paired it with a Vermilion Parish lynching as affairs calling "for more than mere passing mention."

Beyond Louisiana, the Daily Gazette ran a New Orleans dispatch as "Riotous Negroes," subtitled "Firing Into a Pleasure Party of Ladies and Gentlemen." An August 30 wire appeared in the Omaha Daily Bee as "Murderous Negroes," in the Morning Journal and Courier as "A Fatal Row With Negroes," and in Washington's National Republican as "A War of Races." All cast the Black men as "desperate negroes" and "assassins" and gave no account from those arrested.

The Banner said Chenvert was shot "through the heart," the Echo and the wire "through the head." Garon was "seriously wounded" and "may recover" in the Louisiana reports but "mortally wounded" in the wire, whose Omaha headline counted two white men killed. The Banner said the whites were unarmed except Johnson; the wire said they "returned the fire with guns and pistols" and put the arrests at twenty. The Banner, written in the parish within a week, is the closest source, though it too gives only the white side.

bases: An exchange of gunfire at a Black ball in which, by the only (white) accounts, Black men shot first, killing a white man, and a white man's shotgun wounded several Black men, followed by a search and sixteen arrests (A11, A4, A8).

Every report derives from the Pointe Coupee Banner of Aug. 20 or from brief wire dispatches that follow its outline; no account from the Black men at the ball or from court proceedings was found (A11, A4, A7).

accounts.label: Pointe Coupee Banner (local white weekly)
accounts.gist: Black men at the ball, after being warned to keep order, fired on unarmed whites without provocation; Johnson's shotgun dispersed them, wounding several; squads arrested sixteen.

accounts.label: Shreveport and Cincinnati wire
accounts.gist: Black men attacked whites with pistols and the whites 'returned the fire with guns and pistols'; one white killed, one mortally wounded, several Black men shot, twenty arrested.

framing.detail: The Banner called the Black men 'a crowd of desperate negroes' and 'assassins' and reported white determination that 'the guilty shall not escape full measure of punishment'.
The Donaldsonville Chief grouped the affair with a Vermilion lynching under 'Atrocious Crimes' and called the shooters 'the assassins'.
Wire versions ran under 'Murderous Negroes', 'A Fatal Row With Negroes' and 'A War of Races'.
The Daily Gazette's headline read 'Riotous Negroes' with 'Firing Into a Pleasure Party of Ladies and Gentlemen'.

conflicts.note: The Banner's own text (A11) says the heart; the Echo's condensation and the wire say the head.
No report of Garon's death was found; the Omaha Bee headline 'Two White Men Killed' is not supported by its own text.

versions.value: white men returned the fire with guns and pistols

conflicts.note: The local Banner is the closer source, but both come from the white side.
The Banner, written during the arrests, is the better evidence.
The late wire treated stale news as new; the Banner of Aug. 20 is contemporaneous.
